title: Peak Order Hour per Day
description:
For each day, find the **hour of the day with the most orders**. If there is a tie, pick the earlier hour.

**Table: orders** — `order_id`, `order_timestamp` (TIMESTAMP)

Output columns: `order_date`, `order_hour`, `order_count`. Order by `order_date`.
solution_sql: WITH hourly AS (SELECT order_timestamp::DATE AS order_date, EXTRACT(HOUR FROM order_timestamp)::INTEGER AS order_hour, COUNT(*) AS order_count FROM orders GROUP BY order_timestamp::DATE, EXTRACT(HOUR FROM order_timestamp)), ranked AS (SELECT order_date, order_hour, order_count, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY order_date ORDER BY order_count DESC, order_hour ASC) AS rn FROM hourly) SELECT order_date, order_hour, order_count FROM ranked WHERE rn = 1 ORDER BY order_date;

test_cases.description: Jan 15: hour 14 (3 orders) wins; Jan 16: hour 10 (2 orders) wins; Jan 17: hour 11 (3 orders) wins — 3 rows

hints: Cast order_timestamp to DATE with ::DATE and extract the hour with EXTRACT(HOUR FROM order_timestamp).
GROUP BY date and hour to count orders per hour per day, then apply ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY order_date ORDER BY order_count DESC).
Filter WHERE rn = 1 to get the peak hour per day.
explanation: Jan 15: hour 9 has 2 orders, hour 14 has 3 orders → peak = 14. Jan 16: hour 10 has 2 orders, hour 16 has 1 → peak = 10. Jan 17: hour 11 has 3 orders, hour 15 has 1 → peak = 11. ROW_NUMBER with PARTITION BY order_date picks one peak hour per day. Secondary sort on order_hour ASC breaks ties toward the earlier hour.
